Sybil attack.definition: One entity creating many fake identities so a single interest counts many times in a network where identity is free.
Sybil attack.whyItMatters: It is the reason consensus must price identity, and it is the frame that makes PoW and PoS comparable.
confusions: The defence is economic, not technical: make identity costly.
It is not the same as a 51% attack, though it can enable one.

Byzantine fault tolerance.definition: The ability of a distributed system to agree despite members that may be malicious, provided n >= 3f + 1 for f faulty members.
Byzantine fault tolerance.whyItMatters: It explains why BFT systems are small and permissioned, and why permissionless chains use economics instead of quorums.
confusions: Byzantine faults include lying, not just crashing.
The 3f+1 bound is about quorum arithmetic, not about stake.

CAP theorem.definition: Under a network partition a distributed system cannot provide both strong consistency and full availability; it must sacrifice one.
CAP theorem.whyItMatters: It explains why a blockchain halts or isolates rather than accepting a transaction a longer chain may overturn.
confusions: Partition tolerance is not optional at global scale - consistency versus availability is the real choice.

Finality.definition: The point after which a confirmed block cannot be reversed by the protocol.
Finality.whyItMatters: It is the property a settlement network is really buying, and it differs fundamentally between PoW and PoS.
confusions: PoW finality is probabilistic and strengthens with depth.
PoS checkpoints can give deterministic finality.

Reentrancy.definition: A vulnerability where an external call is made before the contract finishes updating its state, allowing the callee to re-enter and act on stale state.
Reentrancy.whyItMatters: It is the highest-value smart-contract bug ever exploited and the most likely vulnerability question.
confusions: The fix is ordering (checks-effects-interactions), or a reentrancy guard.
It is not the same as an overflow or a tx.origin phishing bug.

GHOST.definition: Greedy Heaviest Observed Sub-Tree: a fork-choice rule that follows the child with the greatest accumulated difficulty below it, not the longest chain.
GHOST.whyItMatters: It closes the cheap-chain attack that a naive longest-chain rule would allow.
confusions: It scores subtrees, not chain length.
It is a fork-choice rule, not a consensus algorithm in itself.

topics.name: Double-Spending Problem
topics.definition: Double spending is presenting the same digital coin to two recipients; a blockchain does not prevent the copy, it orders the two spends and rejects the later one.
topics.problem: Digital value is copied perfectly by accident. Without a shared ordering, two conflicting spends can both look valid to different observers.
mechanism: Alice signs a transaction to Bob, then signs a conflicting one to Carol.
Both propagate; different nodes may see them in different orders.
Consensus orders them, so one is included first and the other is rejected as a conflicting nonce.
Confirmations are the safety margin: each new block buries the transaction deeper.
Reversing a spend at depth d means redoing d blocks of work, so finality strengthens with depth.
At six confirmations, an attacker must out-mine six blocks on top of the chain.
terminology: One block mined on top of the transaction's block.
A second spend of the same funds.

examAnswer.question: Explain the double-spend problem and how it is mitigated.
points: Digital value copies perfectly, so two spends can both appear valid.
The chain does not prevent the copy; consensus orders the two spends.
The first accepted spend wins; the conflicting one is rejected.
Confirmations add depth, and each block makes reversal costlier.
Finality is therefore probabilistic and strengthens with depth.
Prevention is economic, not cryptographic.

traps: No blockchain 'prevents' a double spend at the point of signing - it resolves it by ordering.
Say probabilistic finality and explain depth; do not claim instant finality.
A double spend is not the same as a reorg, though a reorg can enable one.
topics.revision: Two conflicting spends -> consensus orders them -> first wins, second rejected -> confirmations add depth -> reversal gets costlier.
recall: Does the chain prevent the duplicate spend?
No - it orders the two spends and rejects the later one.
What do confirmations add?
Depth, which makes reversal progressively more expensive.
What kind of finality does this give?
Probabilistic finality that strengthens with depth.
What must an attacker redo at six confirmations?
Re-mine six blocks on top of the chain.

topics.name: Byzantine Fault Tolerance
topics.definition: Byzantine fault tolerance is the ability to reach agreement despite members that may lie or send contradictory messages, provided n >= 3f + 1 for f faulty members.
topics.problem: Distributed systems assumed nodes fail by crashing. In an open network, a node can stay online and actively deceive, which is a strictly harder problem.
mechanism: Faulty members may lie, stay silent selectively, or send different messages to different peers.
Honest members must outnumber them enough to form a quorum no coalition of liars can fake.
The bound is n >= 3f + 1: with n = 4 you tolerate 1, with n = 7 you tolerate 2, with n = 10 you tolerate 3.
Agreement is reached in rounds of message exchange, not by spending electricity.
Because rounds are expensive in latency, BFT systems stay small and permissioned.
That is why permissionless chains use economic consensus instead.
terminology: A fault that includes arbitrary, possibly malicious behaviour.
The number of agreeing members required.

examAnswer.question: Define Byzantine fault tolerance and derive the 3f + 1 bound.
points: A Byzantine member may lie, not merely crash.
Agreement requires a quorum no coalition of liars can fake.
The bound is n >= 3f + 1, so n = 4 tolerates 1 and n = 7 tolerates 2.
Each extra liar you wish to survive costs three more members.
Agreement comes from rounds of messages, which costs latency.
Hence BFT suits small permissioned sets, not open networks.

traps: Crash faults are not Byzantine faults - the distinction is the whole point.
The bound is on quorum arithmetic, not on stake or hashpower.
Do not claim BFT scales to thousands of anonymous members.
topics.revision: n >= 3f + 1: n=4 -> f=1, n=7 -> f=2, n=10 -> f=3. Rounds of messages, so small permissioned sets.
recall: With n = 10, how many Byzantine members are tolerated?
f = 3, since n >= 3f + 1.
What makes a fault Byzantine?
It may lie or behave arbitrarily, not merely stop.
Why do BFT systems stay small?
Agreement needs rounds of messages, which is latency-expensive.
What do open networks use instead?
Economic consensus: proof of work or proof of stake.

topics.name: Proof-of-Work vs Proof-of-Stake
topics.definition: Both PoW and PoS make identity expensive to stop one entity posing as many; PoW charges burnt electricity and PoS charges locked, slashable capital.
topics.problem: An open network cannot verify identity, so it must price it. Any mechanism that makes participation costly is Sybil-resistant by construction.
mechanism: PoW: block producers must find a hash below the target, so influence costs hardware and energy.
PoW finality is probabilistic and strengthens with confirmations.
PoS: validators lock stake; producing a conflicting block risks the stake being slashed.
PoS uses ordinary servers and can reach deterministic finality at checkpoints.
PoW 51% attack means renting hashpower; PoS 51% means acquiring and risking stake.
Both are only as strong as their economic assumption about the attacker's budget.
terminology: A PoS node needs a recent trusted checkpoint to sync safely.

examAnswer.question: Compare PoW and PoS on security, energy and finality.
points: Both are Sybil-resistance mechanisms: identity is made expensive.
PoW security rests on hashpower; energy cost is high and finality probabilistic.
PoS security rests on stake with slashing; finality can be deterministic.
PoS lowers energy use sharply but introduces weak subjectivity and stake concentration risk.
Attack cost differs: rent hashpower versus buy and risk stake.
Recommendation: PoS for efficiency, provided validator decentralisation holds.

traps: Both are economic; neither is a cryptographic guarantee against a determined majority.
PoS finality is not free - it depends on checkpoint assumptions and weak subjectivity.
Do not say PoS is 'more secure' in the abstract; compare attack costs.
topics.revision: PoW: burnt energy, hardware, probabilistic finality, attack = rent hashpower. PoS: locked stake, servers, checkpoint finality, attack = lose stake.
recall: What is the shared goal of PoW and PoS?
Making identity expensive, to resist Sybil attacks.
What does PoS trade away compared with PoW?
Energy-intensive hashing, in exchange for weak subjectivity and stake concentration risk.
How does finality differ?
PoW is probabilistic and depth-based; PoS can be deterministic at checkpoints.
What does a PoS 51% attacker lose?
The staked capital backing the conflicting blocks.

topics.name: Consistency, Availability & Partition Tolerance (CAP)
topics.definition: CAP states that under a network partition a distributed system cannot provide both strong consistency and full availability, and a blockchain chooses consistency.
topics.problem: A global network will partition. The system must decide in advance what it will refuse to do when it cannot see all peers, or it will silently serve contradictory data.
mechanism: Partition: the network splits into groups that cannot see each other.
Consistency: all nodes agree on one order - no conflicting reads.
Availability: every node answers every request.
Under partition, a strongly consistent system must refuse service on the side that cannot confirm the canonical order.
Blockchains choose consistency: the minority side stops confirming rather than accept a transaction a longer chain later overturns.
Most web applications choose availability and reconcile later.
terminology: A split where groups cannot communicate.

examAnswer.question: Apply CAP to a blockchain design.
points: Partition tolerance is not optional at global scale.
So the real choice is consistency versus availability.
Blockchains choose consistency: one agreed order over always answering.
Under partition, the minority side refuses to confirm rather than risk an overturn.
Cost of that choice is downtime on the minority side.
Web apps typically choose availability and reconcile divergent state later.

traps: Partition tolerance is assumed, not chosen - say what the real trade is.
Choosing consistency means accepting downtime; that is the cost, not a bug.
Do not present CAP as three equal options you can all have.
topics.revision: Partition is a given -> choose consistency (blockchain) or availability (web app). Blockchain halts the minority rather than accept an overturnable tx.
recall: Which two properties actually trade off?
Consistency and availability, because partition tolerance is mandatory.
What does a blockchain sacrifice during a partition?
Availability on the minority side.
Why refuse to confirm on the minority side?
To avoid accepting a transaction a longer chain later overturns.
What do most web apps choose?
Availability, reconciling later.

topics.name: Turing Completeness
topics.definition: The EVM is Turing complete - it has general memory and loops - and gas is what keeps a Turing-complete shared machine from halting the network.
topics.problem: A general-purpose execution environment can compute anything, including a computation that never terminates. On a replicated machine that is fatal.
mechanism: The EVM has bounded but general memory and supports loops, so in principle it computes anything computable.
An infinite loop would stall every node that executed it.
Gas prices every step, so the meter eventually reaches the limit.
On reaching the limit, execution halts and state is reverted.
The capability is therefore unlimited in principle, but every execution is finite and billable.
Consequence: gas converts the halting problem into an economic bound.
terminology: No general method decides whether a program terminates.
The economic bound that replaces halting analysis.

examAnswer.question: Why is EVM Turing complete, and how is that made safe?
points: It has general memory and loops, so it can compute anything computable.
A non-terminating program would stall every validating node.
Gas prices each step, so the meter rises as execution continues.
On reaching the gas limit, execution halts and state is reverted.
So execution is always finite and billable, despite the machine being general.
Gas substitutes an economic bound for the undecidable halting question.

traps: Turing completeness is a capability, not a safety problem by itself - gas is the control.
The revert means state changes are undone, but the fee is still spent.
Do not claim the EVM is bounded in expressiveness; it is bounded in execution cost.
topics.revision: EVM = Turing complete (general memory + loops). Gas meters every step -> limit reached -> halt + revert. Capability unlimited, execution finite.
recall: What makes the EVM Turing complete?
General-purpose memory plus loops.
Why is that dangerous on a replicated machine?
A non-terminating program would stall every node.
What bounds execution?
Gas: the meter reaches the limit and execution reverts.
What still happens on an out-of-gas halt?
State is reverted, but the gas fee is spent.

topics.name: Greedy Heaviest Observed Sub-Tree (GHOST)
topics.definition: GHOST is a fork-choice rule that follows the child with the greatest accumulated difficulty in its subtree, rather than the longest chain.
topics.problem: When the chain forks, following the longest branch lets an attacker build a long chain of cheap blocks to win, because length says nothing about work done.
mechanism: When a fork appears, a node must choose a branch to extend.
Naive rule: longest chain - exploitable by a cheap-chain attack.
GHOST scores each branch by the total difficulty of everything hanging below it.
At each step it greedily follows the heaviest child, which is cheap to compute.
An attacker's chain of many weak blocks therefore loses to a shorter chain of heavy blocks.
Result: resistance to the cheap-chain attack with a simple local rule.
terminology: The rule for picking a branch.

examAnswer.question: Explain GHOST and why it improves on longest-chain.
points: On a fork a node must choose a branch.
Longest-chain is naive: a long branch may contain almost no real work.
GHOST scores a branch by accumulated difficulty in its subtree.
It greedily follows the heaviest child at each step.
So many weak blocks lose to fewer heavy blocks.
It resists the cheap-chain attack while staying cheap to compute.

traps: GHOST scores subtrees, not lengths - the distinction is the entire answer.
It is a fork-choice rule, not a complete consensus protocol.
Greedy does not mean optimal in general graphs; here it is sufficient by design.
topics.revision: Fork -> score each branch by total difficulty below it -> greedy heaviest child. Beats longest-chain against cheap-chain attacks.
recall: Why is longest-chain exploitable?
A long branch can be built from cheap blocks, so length does not prove work.
What does GHOST score?
Total accumulated difficulty of the subtree.
What does greedy mean here?
Follow the heaviest child at each step.
What attack does it close?
The cheap-chain attack.

topics.name: Sybil Attack
topics.definition: A Sybil attack is one entity creating many fake identities so its single interest counts many times, effective wherever identity is free to create.
topics.problem: Any voting or quorum scheme assumes one member is one entity. If membership costs nothing, membership is meaningless.
mechanism: One entity creates many identities.
Identity creation is free, so it floods the membership.
Its single interest now controls many votes or peers.
Defence: make identity cost something scarce, so votes are limited by resources.
PoW charges electricity per identity; PoS charges locked capital.
The threshold becomes economic rather than technical.
terminology: Making identity costly enough that flooding fails.

examAnswer.question: Define a Sybil attack and give the defence.
points: One entity creates many fake identities.
It works wherever identity is free to create.
The entity's single interest controls many votes or peers.
Defence: make identity cost a scarce resource.
PoW uses electricity, PoS uses locked capital.
Sybil resistance is therefore economic, not cryptographic.

traps: Email verification and rate limits are not Sybil resistance in a permissionless chain.
The defence is not better identity documents; it is cost.
Sybil attack and 51% attack differ: one fakes membership, the other seizes majority.
topics.revision: Free identity -> one entity floods membership -> make identity costly (electricity in PoW, stake in PoS) -> flooding becomes expensive.
recall: When does a Sybil attack work?
Wherever identity is free to create.
What is the defence?
Make identity cost a scarce resource.
How does PoW price identity?
In burnt electricity and hardware.
How does PoS price identity?
In locked, slashable capital.

topics.name: Mining Pools and Centralization
topics.definition: A mining pool is one operator aggregating many miners' hashpower and splitting the reward, which creates a centralisation risk because the pool chooses block contents.
topics.problem: Solo mining has terrible variance - months may pass without a block - so rational miners pool. That concentrates the block-building function in a few operators even though the protocol is decentralised.
mechanism: Miners contribute hashpower to a pool and share the reward by work contributed.
The pool operator builds the block, so it decides which transactions are included and in what order.
A pool with a large share can censor, delay or reorder transactions.
Validation may stay widespread while block production concentrates.
Centralisation is therefore a matter of degree, measured in block-production share.
Mitigation is economic and social - miners choosing smaller pools - not cryptographic.
terminology: Fraction of blocks built by one operator.
Refusing to include a valid transaction.

examAnswer.question: Why do mining pools exist, and what centralisation risk do they create?
points: Solo mining has high variance, so miners pool and split rewards.
The pool operator builds the block and chooses its contents.
A large pool can censor, delay or reorder valid transactions.
Validation can remain distributed while production concentrates.
Centralisation is a degree, measured by block-production share.
Mitigation is miner choice, not cryptography.

traps: Do not say the network is centralised - block production is concentrated, validation may not be.
Pools are not malicious by definition; the risk is structural.
This risk is not solved by a protocol change in the short term.
topics.revision: Solo variance -> pool shares reward -> pool builds the block -> chooses contents -> large pool can censor. Risk = concentration of block production.
recall: Why do miners join pools?
Solo mining variance is too high.
What power does the pool operator have?
Choosing which transactions go into the block.
Is decentralisation a boolean?
No - it is a degree, measured by production share.
How is the risk mitigated?
By miners choosing smaller pools, not by cryptography.

topics.name: Smart Contracts Vulnerabilities
topics.definition: Smart-contract vulnerabilities are ordering and trust mistakes: the contract acts on an unchecked value, or hands control to code it does not control before finishing its own work.
topics.problem: A deployed contract cannot be patched quietly. Every bug is permanent and immediately exploitable by anyone who reads the bytecode.
mechanism: Reentrancy: an external call is made before the balance is updated, so the callee re-enters and drains twice. Fix: checks-effects-interactions or a reentrancy guard.
Integer overflow/underflow: unchecked arithmetic wraps. Fix: Solidity 0.8+ reverts automatically; SafeMath before it.
tx.origin phishing: require(tx.origin == owner) is satisfied by a phishing contract. Fix: check msg.sender.
Unchecked external call: the return value of call/send is ignored. Fix: require the success flag.
Front-running: a visible pending action is copied. Fix: commit-reveal.
Timestamp dependence: block.timestamp is miner-influenceable around the margin. Fix: use block.number where possible.
terminology: The original EOA of the transaction.

examAnswer.question: Name the main smart-contract vulnerabilities and the fix for each.
points: Reentrancy: external call before state update; fix with checks-effects-interactions.
Integer overflow/underflow: use checked arithmetic (0.8+ reverts).
tx.origin phishing: check msg.sender instead.
Unchecked external call: verify the returned success flag.
Front-running: commit-reveal instead of exposing the action.
Timestamp dependence: prefer block.number to block.timestamp.

traps: Always pair the vulnerability with its fix - the marks are in the pairing.
Reentrancy is an ordering bug, not a permissions bug.
Solidity 0.8 changed the default arithmetic; say which version you mean.
topics.revision: Reentrancy -> CEI/guard. Overflow -> checked maths. tx.origin -> msg.sender. Unchecked call -> verify return. Front-run -> commit-reveal. Timestamp -> block.number.
recall: What is the fix for reentrancy?
Update state before the external call (checks-effects-interactions), or use a guard.
Why is tx.origin unsafe for authorisation?
A phishing contract in the middle satisfies it; msg.sender is the immediate caller.
How does Solidity 0.8 change overflow handling?
It reverts on overflow by default, replacing SafeMath.
What pattern stops front-running of a visible action?
Commit-reveal.

topics.name: Blockchain Scalability
topics.definition: Blockchain scalability is the trade between what the base layer can process and where execution happens, with Layer 2 moving work off-chain and posting proofs back.
topics.problem: The base layer can only fit so many transactions per block. Making blocks bigger raises the hardware cost of validating, which quietly centralises the network.
mechanism: Layer 1 limits: block size and gas per block bound throughput; raising them raises node requirements.
Layer 2 moves execution off the base chain: state channels, optimistic rollups, zero-knowledge rollups.
Layer 2 posts proofs or compressed data back to Layer 1 for settlement.
Security inheritance depends on data availability: a rollup that posts data to L1 inherits L1 security.
A rollup that keeps data private inherits much less, because users cannot verify it.
Trade: throughput up, but exit and dispute paths now depend on L2 assumptions.
terminology: Execution moved off the base chain.
Batches transactions and posts a proof or data to L1.
Whether L1 can verify what L2 did.

examAnswer.question: Compare Layer 1 and Layer 2 scaling and state the trade-off.
points: Layer 1 throughput is bounded by block size and gas; raising it raises node cost.
Layer 2 moves execution off-chain: channels, optimistic and zk rollups.
L2 posts proofs or data back to L1 for settlement and dispute.
It inherits L1 security only if its data is available on L1.
Private-data rollups inherit much less security, because users cannot verify.
Trade: higher throughput for extra trust assumptions and exit paths.

traps: Bigger blocks are not free scaling - they centralise validation.
Rollups are not automatically as secure as L1; data availability decides.
Do not claim L2 removes the need for L1; it depends on it for settlement.
topics.revision: L1: bounded by block size/gas; bigger blocks centralise. L2: channels/rollups post proofs to L1. Security inherited only if data is on L1.
recall: Why is making blocks bigger not a free fix?
It raises the hardware cost of validating, centralising the network.
What decides whether L2 inherits L1 security?
Whether its data is posted to L1.
Name three Layer 2 approaches.
State channels, optimistic rollups, zero-knowledge rollups.
What does L1 still provide in a layered design?
Ordering, settlement and data availability.
